blocks.content: A domain model is the code representation of how your business actually works the real-world concepts, rules, and relationships that matter to the people using your system. Get the domain model right and everything else becomes easier. Get it wrong and you spend years fighting your own code.
1. What is a Domain Model?

The domain is the real-world subject area your software works in banking, e-commerce, healthcare, logistics. The domain model is the structured representation of that world in code: the objects, their properties, their relationships, and the rules governing them.
It's not about how data is stored. It's not about what an API endpoint looks like. It's purely about capturing the meaning of your business in code.

ANALOGY: ARCHITECTURAL BLUEPRINTS

An architect doesn't start by thinking about what materials are available or how much things cost. They start by understanding what the building needs to do how people move through it, what each room is for, how spaces relate to each other. 

The blueprint captures the intent. The domain model is that blueprint for your software the intent, before any implementation detail enters the picture.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727527188-680660289.png
This diagram illustrates a Domain Model, which is the core business representation used in Domain-Driven Design (DDD).

The gray circle in the center (Domain Model) represents the business domain and contains all the important business concepts and rules of the application. Instead of thinking about databases, APIs, or infrastructure, the focus is on modeling real-world business entities and their relationships.
The Customer entity represents a user of the system and is connected to Identity and Profile, which store customer-specific information.
The Order entity represents a customer's order and contains important attributes such as Items, Status, and Total. These define what an order consists of and its current state.
The Payment entity handles payment-related information and is associated with concepts like Money and Transaction. This part of the model represents how payments are processed and tracked.
The Shipping entity manages delivery information and is connected to Address and Delivery, representing where and how an order is delivered.

The Domain Events section represents important business events that occur within the system. Events such as OrderPlaced and PaymentReceived capture significant business actions. These events can trigger workflows, notifications, or updates in other parts of the system.

The key idea of a Domain Model is that it captures the business language and business rules directly in code. Instead of having generic database tables and CRUD operations, the system is organized around real business concepts like Customer, Order, Payment, Shipping, and Domain Events.
In simple terms, a Domain Model is a blueprint of the business itself, showing the main entities, their relationships, and the important events that occur within the business domain.
ORIGIN: DOMAIN-DRIVEN DESIGN (DDD)

Domain modelling comes from Eric Evans' book Domain-Driven Design (2003). The core idea: the domain model should be the heart of the system, and everything else the database, the UI, the API should be implementation details around it. The model should speak the same language as the business.
2. Domain Model vs Data Model vs DTO
blocks.text: 2. Domain Model vs Data Model vs DTO

blocks.content: These three things are often confused but serve completely different purposes. Mixing them up is one of the most common design mistakes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727527475-890731809.png
ANALOGY: A HOSPITAL
The domain model is the doctor's understanding of the patient symptoms, diagnosis, treatment plan, rules about what drugs interact.
The data model is the hospital's database schema patient records table, appointments table, prescriptions table.
The DTO is the printed discharge summary handed to the patient a trimmed, readable version of what they need to know. Three representations of the same reality, each designed for a different purpose.
3. Building Blocks of a Domain Model
blocks.text: 3. Building Blocks of a Domain Model

blocks.content: DDD defines a set of standard building blocks for expressing domain models. Each one has a specific role and specific rules about how it behaves.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727527887-111318390.png

["Entity is a business object with a unique identity that remains the same even if its data changes. Examples are Customer, Order, and Product.
","Value Object has no identity and is defined only by its values. Examples are Address, Money, and Email.
","Aggregate is a group of related objects managed as a single unit through one root object. For example, an Order and its OrderItems.
","Domain Service contains business logic that doesn't belong to a single object. For example, a PricingService that calculates discounts.
","Domain Event represents something important that happened in the system, such as OrderPlaced or PaymentReceived.
","Repository is responsible for loading and saving domain objects while hiding database details from the business logic."]
items: Entity is a business object with a unique identity that remains the same even if its data changes. Examples are Customer, Order, and Product.
Value Object has no identity and is defined only by its values. Examples are Address, Money, and Email.
Aggregate is a group of related objects managed as a single unit through one root object. For example, an Order and its OrderItems.
Domain Service contains business logic that doesn't belong to a single object. For example, a PricingService that calculates discounts.
Domain Event represents something important that happened in the system, such as OrderPlaced or PaymentReceived.
Repository is responsible for loading and saving domain objects while hiding database details from the business logic.

blocks.content: 4. Entities in the Domain
An entity represents a distinct thing that has identity something you track over time because which specific one matters. It has a unique ID that never changes, even as its attributes do.
The critical question: does it matter which specific one it is, or just what it is? If it matters which specific one it's an entity.

ANALOGY: A PARCEL IN A DELIVERY SYSTEM

Two parcels can be identical in weight, size, and contents but they're going to different addresses. Which specific parcel matters enormously. Each parcel has a tracking ID, a history of locations, and a recipient. It is an entity. The weight printed on the label? That's just a value.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: KEY POINT: BUSINESS RULES BELONG TO THE ENTITY

Notice that cancel() is a method on Order, not in an OrderService. The rule "a shipped order can't be cancelled" is a domain rule it belongs in the domain model, not scattered across services. This is what makes a rich domain model vs an anemic domain model (covered in S11).
5. Value Objects in the Domain
A value object represents a descriptive aspect of the domain with no conceptual identity. Two value objects with the same attributes are identical and interchangeable. They are always immutable.

Value objects are not just for wrapping primitives they carry domain meaning and enforce domain rules. A Money object knows it can't be negative. An EmailAddress knows what a valid email looks like. These rules belong in the value object, not in a validator elsewhere.
Money and EmailAddress are Value Objects because they represent a value, not a business entity.
Money stores an amount and currency, validates business rules (like no negative money), and is immutable. Operations such as add() return a new Money object instead of changing the existing one.
EmailAddress stores an email value and ensures only valid email addresses can be created.
They are Value Objects because they:
["Have no ID","Are defined by their values","Are immutable","Contain domain validation rules"]
items: Have no ID
Are defined by their values
Are immutable
Contain domain validation rules

blocks.content: Easy rule:

Customer, Order → Entity (has identity)
Money, EmailAddress, Address → Value Object (represents a value)

UsingMoneyinstead ofdoubleorBigDecimal prevents a whole class of bugs: you can never accidentally add USD to INR, you can never store a negative price, and the domain intent is self-documenting. Replace primitives with value objects wherever a domain concept exists.
6. Aggregates: Grouping Related Objects

An aggregate is a cluster of related entities and value objects treated as a single unit. One entity in the cluster is designated the Aggregate Root the only entry point into the aggregate from outside.
The aggregate root enforces all invariants (rules that must always be true) for the entire cluster. You never directly access or modify an object inside an aggregate you always go through the root.

ANALOGY: A COMPANY AND ITS DEPARTMENTS

You don't walk directly into the Finance department and reorganise it. You go through the CEO. 

The CEO (aggregate root) coordinates all changes to the company's internal structure (entities and value objects inside the aggregate). Direct access to internal components bypasses the rules the CEO is responsible for enforcing.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727528005-735579761.png
This diagram shows an Aggregate in Domain-Driven Design.
The Order Aggregate is the boundary that groups related objects together. Inside it, the Order Root is the Aggregate Root, which acts as the main entry point.
The OrderItem Entity and ShippingAddress Value Object belong to the Order Aggregate, but external code cannot access them directly.
The External system must interact only with the Order Root. The Order Root then manages and validates changes to OrderItems and ShippingAddress.
For example, instead of directly adding an OrderItem:
External → OrderItem
You do:
External → Order Root → OrderItem
This ensures all business rules are enforced in one place.
AGGREGATE RULES

["Only the aggregate root has a global identity (ID stored in the DB). Internal entities may have local IDs only meaningful within the aggregate. 
","Nothing outside the aggregate boundary holds a reference to an internal entity only to the root. 
","A single transaction should only modify one aggregate. Cross-aggregate changes happen through domain events.
"]
items: Only the aggregate root has a global identity (ID stored in the DB). Internal entities may have local IDs only meaningful within the aggregate.
Nothing outside the aggregate boundary holds a reference to an internal entity only to the root.
A single transaction should only modify one aggregate. Cross-aggregate changes happen through domain events.

blocks.content: 7. Domain Services
Some domain logic doesn't naturally belong to a single entity or value object it involves multiple objects or represents a standalone operation in the domain. This is where domain services come in.
A domain service is not an application service (which orchestrates use cases). It's a piece of business logic that has no natural home in an entity or value object.

ANALOGY: A CURRENCY EXCHANGE COUNTER

Converting USD to INR doesn't belong to the USD note it's not an operation that a single currency object can perform on its own. It requires exchange rate knowledge and involves two currencies.

A currency exchange counter (domain service) performs the operation. The domain service is the counter a stateless process that takes inputs from multiple objects and produces a result.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: Domain service vs Application service: A domain service contains pure business logic it has no idea about HTTP, databases, or external systems. An application service orchestrates: it calls repositories, calls domain services, and coordinates the flow. If your "domain service" calls a repository or sends an email, it's actually an application service.
8. Domain Events
A domain event represents something significant that happened in the domain a fact that is immutable and in the past. Events are named in past tense: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, ItemShipped.

They decouple aggregates from each other. Instead of Order directly calling the Inventory service, Order fires an OrderPlaced event. Anyone who cares about that Inventory, Notifications, Analytics subscribes and reacts independently.

ANALOGY: A NEWSPAPER

When a company goes public, it doesn't call every investor individually. It publishes the news in a newspaper (fires the event). Anyone who subscribed reads it and takes their own action. Some buy shares, some update spreadsheets, some write articles. The company doesn't know or care who is listening it just publishes the fact.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727528224-527992626.png
A Domain Event is simply a record that says "something important happened in the business."
In this diagram, OrderPlaced is the event.
When an order is placed, the system announces:
"An order has been placed."
Other parts of the system listen to this event and take action:
["Send Email","Update Inventory","Create Shipment"]
items: Send Email
Update Inventory
Create Shipment

blocks.content: The order service doesn't need to know about these actions. It just publishes the event, and other services react to it.
Easy way to remember:

OrderPlaced = What happened?
Send Email, Update Inventory, Create Shipment = What should happen next?
So, a Domain Event is a business notification that something important has already happened.
9. Repositories: Accessing the Domain

A repository provides the illusion that you have an in-memory collection of domain objects. It hides all the database details SQL, JPA, network calls from the domain model. The domain only sees a clean collection interface.

ANALOGY: A LIBRARY CATALOGUE

When you ask a librarian "do you have any books on distributed systems?", you don't need to know which shelf they're on, which database they use, or how the catalogue is organised. 

You get the books. The repository is the librarian an interface that gives your domain objects without exposing how or where they're stored.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727528317-547469747.png
A Repository acts as a bridge between the Domain Model and the Database. The domain model does not directly interact with database tables or SQL queries. Instead, it communicates with the repository.
When the application needs to save or retrieve an object such as an Order or Customer, it asks the Repository. The Repository then handles all database operations behind the scenes.
For example, instead of writing:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 1
inside business logic, you simply call:
orderRepository.findById(1)
The Repository fetches the data from the database and returns a domain object.
The Repository hides database details so the domain focuses only on business rules.
ONE REPOSITORY PER AGGREGATE ROOT

You create a repository for the aggregate root not for every entity inside the aggregate. There's an OrderRepository, not an OrderItemRepository. OrderItems are accessed through their root Order. This enforces aggregate boundaries at the persistence level too.
10. A Complete Example: E-Commerce Order Domain
blocks.text: 10. A Complete Example: E-Commerce Order Domain

blocks.content: Putting it all together. Here's what a well-modelled e-commerce order domain looks like, using all six building blocks.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780727528416-376297285.png
This diagram shows how all Domain-Driven Design (DDD) building blocks work together in a real-world E-Commerce Order System.

At the center is the Order Aggregate Root, which is the main business object. Whenever someone places an order, all changes must go through the Order Aggregate Root. It acts as the gatekeeper of the entire Order Aggregate.
The Customer Entity represents the customer placing the order. It is an Entity because it has a unique identity (Customer ID) that remains the same even if customer details change.

["The OrderItem Entity represents products inside the order. Each order item has its own identity and belongs to the Order Aggregate.
","The Money Value Object represents prices and amounts. It has no identity and is defined only by its value, such as ₹500 or $20.
","The ShippingAddress Value Object represents where the order should be delivered. Since an address is just a value and has no identity, it is modeled as a Value Object.
","The Pricing Service (Domain Service) contains business logic that doesn't naturally belong to a single object. For example, calculating discounts, taxes, coupon codes, or final pricing. Instead of putting this logic inside Order or Customer, it is placed in a Domain Service.
","The Order Repository is responsible for saving and loading Order Aggregates from the database. The Order Aggregate never talks directly to the database. It uses the Repository.
"]
items: The OrderItem Entity represents products inside the order. Each order item has its own identity and belongs to the Order Aggregate.
The Money Value Object represents prices and amounts. It has no identity and is defined only by its value, such as ₹500 or $20.
The ShippingAddress Value Object represents where the order should be delivered. Since an address is just a value and has no identity, it is modeled as a Value Object.

The Pricing Service (Domain Service) contains business logic that doesn't naturally belong to a single object. For example, calculating discounts, taxes, coupon codes, or final pricing. Instead of putting this logic inside Order or Customer, it is placed in a Domain Service.
The Order Repository is responsible for saving and loading Order Aggregates from the database. The Order Aggregate never talks directly to the database. It uses the Repository.

blocks.content: When the order is successfully created, an OrderPlaced Domain Event is generated. This event tells the rest of the system:
"An order has been placed."
Other services can then react to this event, such as:
["Sending a confirmation email","Updating inventory","Creating a shipment","Generating an invoice"]
items: Sending a confirmation email
Updating inventory
Creating a shipment
Generating an invoice

blocks.content: So the complete flow is:

Customer places an order → Pricing Service calculates price → Order Aggregate creates and validates the order → Repository saves the order → OrderPlaced event is published → Other systems react to the event.
This diagram combines all six DDD building blocks:
["Entity → Customer, OrderItem","Value Object → Money, ShippingAddress","Aggregate → Order Aggregate","Domain Service → Pricing Service","Repository → Order Repository","Domain Event → OrderPlaced"]
items: Entity → Customer, OrderItem
Value Object → Money, ShippingAddress
Aggregate → Order Aggregate
Domain Service → Pricing Service
Repository → Order Repository
Domain Event → OrderPlaced

blocks.content: In one sentence:

The Order Aggregate sits at the center of the domain, uses Value Objects and Entities to represent business data, Domain Services for business logic, Repositories for persistence, and Domain Events to notify the rest of the system when something important happens.
11. Common Mistakes
Even with the right DDD concepts, a few common mistakes can make the domain model difficult to maintain, scale, and evolve.
Mistake 1: Anemic Domain Model

The most common and most damaging mistake. Classes have only fields and getters/setters all the logic lives in services. The domain model is a dumb data bag. This is essentially procedural programming dressed up as OOP.
ANEMIC: ORDER HAS NO BEHAVIOUR, LOGIC IS SCATTERED IN SERVICES
RICH DOMAIN MODEL: RULES LIVE IN THE OBJECT
Mistake 2: Domain model aware of persistence
blocks.text: Mistake 2: Domain model aware of persistence

blocks.content: Adding JPA annotations (@Entity, @Column) directly on domain objects couples your business model to the database.
A change in the DB schema forces a change in the domain object, and vice versa. Keep them separate use a dedicated persistence model.
Mistake 3: Crossing aggregate boundaries directly

Holding a direct object reference to an entity inside another aggregate instead of referencing it by ID breaks aggregate isolation. The second aggregate can now bypass the first aggregate's rules by modifying its internal entities directly.
WRONG: ORDER HOLDS A DIRECT REFERENCE TO CUSTOMER'S ADDRESS
CORRECT: COPY THE ADDRESS VALUE INTO THE ORDER
Mistake 4: One giant aggregate
Putting everything into one large aggregate
(Customer + Order + Product + Inventory all in one) creates a massive lock contention problem.
Every write to any part of the aggregate locks the whole thing. Keep aggregates small only group objects that truly need to be consistent together.
12. Summary

["A domain model is a code representation of business concepts, rules, and relationships not about storage or APIs, purely about meaning.","Entity: has a unique ID, identity persists through changes, equality by ID. Business rules live as methods on the entity not in services.","Value Object: no ID, defined by attributes, immutable. Enforces domain rules at construction. Use records in Java. Replace raw primitives with meaningful VOs.","Aggregate: cluster of related objects with one root. All access goes through the root. Root enforces all invariants. One repository per aggregate root. Keep aggregates small.","Domain Service: stateless logic that doesn't fit in one entity or value object. Contains business logic only no DB calls, no HTTP.","Domain Event: an immutable fact that something happened in the domain, named in past tense. Decouples aggregates from each other.","Repository: hides persistence details from the domain. Domain sees a clean collection interface. One repository per aggregate root. Interface in domain layer; implementation in infrastructure layer.","Avoid the anemic domain model classes should have behaviour (methods encoding business rules), not just fields and setters.","Keep aggregates small, cross-aggregate references by ID only, and use domain events to coordinate across aggregate boundaries.","The domain model must not know about databases, HTTP, or external systems those are implementation details that live outside the domain layer."]
items: A domain model is a code representation of business concepts, rules, and relationships not about storage or APIs, purely about meaning.
Entity: has a unique ID, identity persists through changes, equality by ID. Business rules live as methods on the entity not in services.
Value Object: no ID, defined by attributes, immutable. Enforces domain rules at construction. Use records in Java. Replace raw primitives with meaningful VOs.
Aggregate: cluster of related objects with one root. All access goes through the root. Root enforces all invariants. One repository per aggregate root. Keep aggregates small.
Domain Service: stateless logic that doesn't fit in one entity or value object. Contains business logic only no DB calls, no HTTP.
Domain Event: an immutable fact that something happened in the domain, named in past tense. Decouples aggregates from each other.
Repository: hides persistence details from the domain. Domain sees a clean collection interface. One repository per aggregate root. Interface in domain layer; implementation in infrastructure layer.
Avoid the anemic domain model classes should have behaviour (methods encoding business rules), not just fields and setters.
Keep aggregates small, cross-aggregate references by ID only, and use domain events to coordinate across aggregate boundaries.
The domain model must not know about databases, HTTP, or external systems those are implementation details that live outside the domain layer.
